how-much-to-invest-by-age.title: How much you should invest each month by age (and what to do if you're starting late)
how-much-to-invest-by-age.excerpt: Compound interest turns every year of delay into a lot more monthly effort. Here are rough figures by age, where to put that money, and what to do if you're starting late.

imageAlt.snowball: Three people pushing a snowball downhill: at 20-25 with little effort, at 35 with more effort, and at 45-50 with much more effort, heading towards a "financial freedom" flag.
imageAlt.startToday: One person sitting and wondering if saving €50 is enough, and another person climbing a staircase of growing savings jars (€50, €100, €200+) towards a flag that reads "future you will thank you".

blocks.p: Many people try to manage their money responsibly: they avoid unnecessary debt, keep some margin at the end of the month, and intend to start investing "later on". The problem is that in finance, time has a very concrete value.
Waiting five or ten years doesn't just push back the date you reach financial peace of mind; it radically changes how much you need to put in from your own pocket every month.

sections.heading: The effect of time on your money

blocks.p: Compound interest is the engine that makes an investment grow over the long term. It works in a very simple way: the returns your money generates get reinvested and start generating returns of their own.
To understand the difference time makes, consider two hypothetical cases with an estimated average return of 8% a year:

list: **Starting at 25:** if you invest €200 a month from age 25 to 65, you'll have contributed €96,000 out of your own pocket. By the end of the period, compound interest will have turned that money into roughly €580,000.

**Starting at 35:** if you wait ten years and decide to make up for it by investing double (€400 a month) until 65, you'll have contributed €144,000 out of your own pocket. Yet the final result is only around €450,000.

blocks.p: Even though you contributed more money each month, the result is lower because the money had ten fewer years to multiply.

sections.heading: Where to put this money in a simple way

blocks.p: You don't need to analyze charts every day or chase the trendiest company. For most people with a full-time job, the most efficient and diversified option is index funds.
An index fund is a basket that tracks a whole index (like the S&P 500 or the MSCI World). Its main advantages are:

orderedList: **Automatic diversification:** your money is spread across hundreds or thousands of companies instead of depending on just one.
**Low costs:** fees tend to be very low (around 0.20% a year).
**Tax efficiency (in Spain):** you can move money from one fund to another without being taxed until you actually withdraw it.

blocks.p: Getting started just takes opening an account with a specialized broker (such as MyInvestor, Trade Republic or Interactive Brokers) and setting up an automatic monthly transfer.

sections.heading: What to do if you're starting late or earning less

blocks.p: If you look at the figures for your age bracket and can't reach those numbers, that doesn't mean you should give up on investing. Having €100,000 or €300,000 saved by retirement will always give you more room and peace of mind than having nothing.
There are five ways to adjust the plan to your situation:

orderedList: **Increase your income:** finding ways to earn more (changing jobs, negotiating a raise, developing skills) is usually more effective than constantly cutting basic expenses.
**Start with what you have today:** if you can only set aside €50 or €100 a month, start there. Building the habit makes it easier to increase the amount as your income grows.
**Adjust your expectations:** focus on supplementing your future pension rather than fixating on one exact figure.
**Allocate a small part to higher-potential assets:** with the right knowledge, a very small share of the portfolio (5%-10%) can go to alternative assets, accepting a higher level of risk.
**Extend your time horizon:** working or keeping your investments until age 68 or 70 adds years of compound growth and reduces the number of retirement years to fund.

callout.text: What if you push back your retirement age or change your monthly contribution? Play with the parameters in our Compound Interest Calculator to find a realistic scenario that fits your current lifestyle.

list: **Waiting for the "perfect moment":** the best time to start was ten years ago; the second best time is today.

**Trying to time the market:** nobody knows if the market will go up or down next month. Investing a fixed amount on a regular basis (dollar-cost averaging) averages out purchases across highs and lows.
**Selling during a downturn:** temporary drops of 10% or 20% are common in the markets. Selling out of panic turns a temporary loss into a permanent one.
**Investing in products you don't understand:** if you don't understand how a financial product works or what it costs, don't put your money into it.
**Not automating it:** relying on remembering every month means any unexpected expense can push the investment back. Set up the transfer for the day after you get paid.

orderedList: Look at your income and expenses for the month.
Set a fixed amount you can afford without straining your day-to-day budget.
Open an investment account and choose a global or diversified fund.
Set up an automatic monthly transfer so the process runs on its own.
